All topics · Indian History · Lesson 7

The Guptas and the "Golden Age"

Two sittings (read ~25 min one day, lesson ~25 min the next). You can describe how the Gupta empire was built (a core ruled directly, rings of tributary kings), and weigh the label "Golden Age" against the evidence, for and against.

Why this lesson

Five centuries after the Maurya empire ended, a second dynasty from the Ganges plain built an empire across northern India: the Guptas (c. AD 320–500). Nationalist historians of the early twentieth century called their age India's "Golden Age": peace, prosperity, Sanskrit poetry, the Puranas, and the name stuck. K&R print the phrase in quotation marks. The question to carry through: golden by what evidence, and golden for whom?

You'll meet two familiar problems again. Much of the evidence is royal self-praise, as with Ashoka's edicts. And one of the best outside witnesses, a Chinese monk, looked mainly at what interested him: Buddhism.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Both questions use only earlier lessons.

Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII says he felt deep remorse for the Kalinga war. Which statement best describes the edict as a source on that remorse?

The words are certain: they're cut in stone at many sites. But they are the king's own account, written for an audience he chose (it was left out at the two sites in Kalinga itself). The people of Kalinga left no account. The same two questions apply to the Gupta king's inscription in this lesson.

Put these in order, earliest first.

c. 320 BC → 261 BC → 185 BC (lessons 5 and 6). Today's lesson starts about five centuries after the last of these, in AD 320.

Recap: the circle of kings, and reading a royal source
  • Rajamandala, "the circle of kings" (lesson 5): the Arthashastra's picture of a king surrounded by rings of other kings. Your neighbour is your natural enemy, your neighbour's neighbour your natural friend. K&R use the same word for the Gupta empire's rings of power.
  • Who speaks, for whom, why? (lessons 5 and 6): the Rigveda gives the priests' view; Ashoka's edicts give the king's view. A royal inscription is reliable about what the king wanted said, not about how others saw it.
  • Corroboration (lesson 5): two sources with different authors and different purposes agree.

Block 1: read first

Reading

Kulke & Rothermund, A History of India, Chapter Two, "The classical age of the Guptas": from the start of that section to the end of "An age of religious tolerance and political consolidation", stopping at "Internal and external challenges: Pushyamitras and Huns". About 8 pages, including the two boxed quotations, "Samudragupta – 'a god dwelling on earth'?" and "A Chinese report on casteism and the 'Golden Age' of the Guptas", and Map 2.3.

Optional, if you want the trade side: the later section "India's flourishing 'Rome trade'" in the same chapter.

Name traps:

  • Two Chandraguptas. Chandragupta Maurya (c. 320 BC) founded the Maurya dynasty. Chandragupta I (AD 320) and Chandragupta II (c. AD 375–413/415) are Guptas, unrelated.
  • Two Pushyamitras. Pushyamitra Shunga (185 BC) is the general from lesson 6. "The Pushyamitras" in the next section, just after where you stop, are a tribe on the Narmada in the 5th century AD. Unrelated; you can stop before them.
  • Prasasti = a eulogy, a praise-poem for a king. Digvijaya = "conquest of the four quarters", a ritual tour of conquest. Ashvamedha = the Vedic horse sacrifice. Faxian is also spelled Fa-hsien or Fahsien.

Samudragupta's Allahabad inscription sorts the rulers he dealt with into groups. Name the groups, and for each say what he got from them.

Core: kings "uprooted", realms annexed and ruled by royal officers. Border kings: paid tribute, obeyed orders, attended court (not obliged to fight for him). Forest/jungle rajas: claimed as servants, probably no tribute; at most kept from disturbing the core. Independent kings beyond (Kushanas, Shakas, Sri Lanka, "all islands"): embassies, gifts, requests for charters; diplomatic relations only. The southern kings: defeated, released and reinstated. Any three groups. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

What does Faxian report about life in northern India, and why do K&R warn that his report is limited?

Rich and contented people, no poll tax, only cultivators of the king's land pay land tax and they may go or stay; no capital punishment, light or heavy fines; officials receive salaries; no killing, wine, onion or garlic, except the Chandalas, segregated, who strike a piece of wood when entering towns or markets. Limited: he was only interested in Buddhism, so his report has little political information. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

Two kinds of religious donations appear in "An age of religious tolerance…". Which were more secure, and why do K&R say the land grants mattered for later history?

Gold coins to Buddhist monasteries (interest funded monks, lamps, buildings) depended on rich townspeople and suffered when towns declined; land grants to Brahmins and temples, or the revenue of whole villages, were more secure. The grants (copper plates, 433–449 in Bengal) are among the earliest examples of what became the basis of "Indian feudalism"; mostly uncultivated land, so grantees extended agriculture. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

What surprised or confused you in the reading? (Optional.)

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

1. How the empire was built: rings, not a block (from the reading)

| Ruler | Dates (K&R) | What K&R stress | |---|---|---| | Chandragupta I | AD 320 – c. 335 | married a Licchavi princess; new era from his coronation in 320 | | Samudragupta | c. 335–75 | the conqueror; the Allahabad inscription; the horse sacrifice | | Chandragupta II | c. 375–413/415 | the empire's height; took Gujarat from the Shakas; marriage alliance with the Vakatakas; Faxian's visit | | Kumaragupta | 415–55 | peace and consolidation; religious endowments; the provincial administration |

Start from the source. Almost everything about Samudragupta's conquests comes from one undated inscription, cut on an old Ashokan pillar now at Allahabad. It is a prasasti, a praise-poem: the box in your reading calls him "a god, dwelling on earth". So, as with Ashoka: reliable about what the king claimed, not about how far his power really reached.

What it claims. Four kinds of relationship, in rings around the centre:

  1. The core: kings "uprooted" in the Ganges plain, between west Bengal, Mathura and Vidisha. Annexed, and ruled by royal officers.
  2. Border kings (Samatata in southeast Bengal, Kamarupa in Assam, Nepal, tribes in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh): paid tribute, followed orders, came to court. But unlike European vassals, they did not have to fight in his army.
  3. Forest rulers in the Vindhyas: claimed as his "servants"; probably no tribute at all.
  4. Independent kings beyond (the Kushanas, the Shakas, Sri Lanka, "all islands"): sent embassies and gifts. Diplomacy only.

The southern campaign doesn't fit any ring. Twelve southern kings were "defeated, released and reinstated". K&R read this as a euphemism: conquest for prestige, not annexation, since such distant realms couldn't have been controlled anyway. The southern kings went on ruling undisturbed.

Why it matters. K&R call this structure "a blueprint for all medieval kingdoms of India". Compare the Mauryas (lesson 6): a core ruled directly plus four provinces under princes as viceroys, with an unconquered interior. The Gupta empire had a directly ruled core too, but around it tributary kings who kept their thrones, not provinces. Some historians call it "multicentred" rather than unitary.

Sort each ruler by Samudragupta's relationship with him, as the Allahabad inscription presents it.

The core kings were "uprooted". Kamarupa is in the list of border kings who paid tribute and came to court. The Kushanas were beyond his reach but wanted good relations. Kanchipuram was the last stop of the southern campaign, whose kings were "defeated, released and reinstated".

How did Samudragupta's border kings differ from vassals in medieval Europe, according to K&R?

Tribute (kara), following orders (ajna) and obedience shown by attending court (pramana), yes; military service, no. K&R: "not real vassals but, at the most, tributary princes". Only later, as samantas, did such rulers come closer to the feudal vassal.

The Allahabad inscription lists Sri Lanka among the realms that showed Samudragupta their obedience. What does the separate Chinese report about Sri Lanka add? (Not Faxian's: K&R don't name this source.)

An independent source (different author, different purpose) agrees that there was contact: King Meghavanna sent an embassy asking permission to build a monastery and a pilgrims' guesthouse at Bodh Gaya. Samudragupta counted the presents as tribute, as a Chinese emperor would have. Corroboration of the contact, and a correction of its meaning: "diplomatic relations… without any effect on the actual exercise of political control".

2. Dating by coins (from the reading)

A conquest with no recorded date. Chandragupta II took the Shaka kingdom in Gujarat, but no source says when. K&R date it from coins alone.

Two dated coin issues. The Shaka ruler Rudrasimha III issued coins in 397, so he still ruled then. Chandragupta II issued coins of the same Shaka pattern in 409, but with the Shakas' Buddhist vihara replaced by Garuda, Vishnu's eagle and the Gupta symbol. A Gupta king copying a local coin type means he now ruled where that type was used.

So the conquest falls between 397 and 409. A dated coin gives a floor ("still ruling then") or a ceiling ("already conquered by then"); two of them bracket the event.

A Shaka-style coin of a Gupta king is dated 409. What does that coin by itself show about the conquest of Gujarat?

A Gupta king minting the local type means he already ruled there: a ceiling, not a date. The floor (397) comes from a different coin, the last dated one of the Shaka ruler Rudrasimha III. K&R: "the date of this event is not recorded", so the two coins are all we have.

3. "Golden" by what evidence? (from the reading)

The case for. From your reading:

  • Money and trade: many gold coins (dinara, first on the Roman pattern), silver coins after the Shaka conquest; direct access to eastern and western ports; prosperous guilds of bankers, traders and artisans, some running parts of towns.
  • Order: Faxian's peace: no death penalty (fines instead, though plotters of treason lost their right hand), no poll tax, salaried officials and free peasants.
  • Culture: classical Sanskrit literature under royal patronage (Kalidasa), the Puranas taking final shape, Gupta sculpture such as the Varaha relief at Udayagiri.
  • Tolerance: endowments to Buddhist and Jain sites as well as to Vishnu, Shiva, Skanda, Surya and Shakti "abound in all parts of the empire".

The case against, also from your reading:

  • Caste. The same Faxian box: the Chandalas, called "evil men", were segregated and had to strike a piece of wood when entering towns or markets so others could avoid them. K&R: the treatment of untouchables was "very similar" to later periods.
  • Whose voice? The grandest evidence is royal propaganda ("a god dwelling on earth"); the Guptas "consciously strove to renew the old Hindu institutions of kingship"; Kalidasa's epics may turn the dynasty's history into myth.
  • Decline inside the period. Towns, and the Buddhist monasteries that depended on their rich citizens, declined in the late Gupta period.
  • A narrow witness. Faxian "was only interested in Buddhism", so his report has little political information.

Beyond the reading, my own reading of it: the land grants to Brahmins, which K&R call the basis of the concept of "Indian feudalism", are read by some historians as a cost (land and the people on it passing to grantees). K&R themselves stress that the grantees extended agriculture. Weigh it yourself.

What K&R do with Faxian. They use his evidence against a different claim: that rigid untouchability arose in India only as a reaction to the Islamic conquest. Centuries before any Islamic conquest of India, it is already in Faxian's description.

Faxian's report, as quoted in your reading. Click the sentence(s) showing that one group was shut out of the life Faxian describes.

The region to the South is known as the Middle Kingdom. The people are rich and contented, unencumbered by any poll-tax or official restrictions. Only those who till the king's land pay a land tax, and they are free to go or stay as they please. The kings govern without recourse to capital punishment, but offenders are fined lightly or heavily according to the nature of their crime. Even those who plot high treason only have their right hands cut off. The king's attendants and retainers all receive emoluments and pensions. The people in this country kill no living creatures, drink no wine, and eat no onion or garlic. [[The single exception to this is the Chandalas, who are known as 'evil men' and are segregated from the others.]] [[When they enter towns or markets they strike a piece of wood to announce their presence, so that others may know they are coming and avoid them.]]

The last two sentences: "the single exception" is an exception to the rule just before it (no killing, no wine, no onion or garlic). They describe a group outside the "rich and contented" people: segregated, named "evil men", and made to announce themselves so others could avoid them. (Faxian, A Record of the Buddhist Countries, tr. Shan Shih, quoted in K&R.)

Sort each piece of evidence from the reading: does it support calling the Gupta age "golden", or count against it?

Tolerance and prosperous guilds are the strongest "for" evidence; segregation of the Chandalas and the late urban decline cut against it. The label hides who it was golden for, and when.

Beyond the reading: the label itself has a history. Historians such as D. D. Kosambi and Romila Thapar have questioned it. The historian Kesavan Veluthat argues it was built by nationalist historians in the early twentieth century, when a glorious past encouraged an educated middle class under colonial rule. In his summary of Kosambi: "rather than the Guptas reviving Indian nationalism, Indian nationalism revived the Guptas!" That's one side of an argument, and the article is in Extra practice below.

The claim: "The Gupta age was India's Golden Age." Using the reading, give (1) two pieces of evidence that support the claim, (2) one piece of evidence against it or limiting it, and (3) one reason to be careful with the source behind a piece of evidence you used. Then give your verdict in a sentence: golden for whom?

Grades exactly the three named parts, from the reading only. (1) Any two: gold (and silver) coins and growing trade; guilds; Faxian's peace, no death penalty, no poll tax, free peasants, salaried officials; classical Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa) and the Puranas; endowments to many religions; the administrative system. (2) Any one: Faxian's Chandalas (segregation, untouchability); late decline of towns and monasteries; mutilation for treason; the southern "conquests" were for show; land grants to Brahmins, if argued as a cost. (3) Any one, matched to evidence they used: the Allahabad inscription is royal praise (a prasasti); Faxian was interested only in Buddhism, a pilgrim's view; coins served as propaganda (god-like portrayals); Kalidasa wrote under royal patronage. Verdict: any reasoned verdict. Got it = all three parts, no false statement. Naming Kosambi, Thapar or Veluthat earns credit, never required.

Extra practice (optional)

  • Reading: the Samudragupta box once more. List every claim in it that a second, independent source could check, and say what kind of source would do it (a coin, a foreign report, an excavation).
  • Extra reading: Faxian's own account, whole: James Legge's 1886 translation, A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, chapter XVI (on "the Middle Kingdom"), free on Project Gutenberg. A different translation from the one K&R quote, so compare the wording on the Chandalas.
  • Extra article: Kesavan Veluthat, "The myth of the Gupta Empire as the 'Golden Age' for India", a short 1997 lecture reprinted by SabrangIndia from Communalism Combat (about 520 words), sabrangindia.in. A historian's case that the label was made in the twentieth century, drawing on land rights, the position of women and shudras, and Buddhist art of the period. It argues one side, in a magazine with a stated political mission, so weigh it the way the lesson weighs the Allahabad inscription.
